s1.syndrome_frame: Chronic skin ulcer with areas of healthy skin and genetic alterations in a collagen gene
salient_findings: Large unhealed ulcer on the back
Patch of healthy skin on the left forearm
key_facts: Patient is a 30-year-old woman
Ulcer has persisted for 3 years
Ulcer measures 20 × 14-cm²
Patch of healthy skin measures 7.5 × 4 cm²
Blood cell genotyping showed compound heterozygous alterations in COL7A1
RNA transcript analysis showed dominant RNA transcripts with premature stop codons in affected skin epidermis
Potentially revertant area epidermis had high rates of wild-type transcripts
Immunofluorescence and transmission electron microscopy showed type VII collagen and anchoring fibrils

s4.champion: Revertant Mosaicism in Dystrophic Epidermolysis Bullosa

raw.champion: Revertant Mosaicism in Dystrophic Epidermolysis Bullosa
raw.rationale: The presence of a large unhealed ulcer and a patch of healthy skin, along with genetic testing showing compound heterozygous alterations in COL7A1 and RNA transcript analysis revealing dominant RNA transcripts with premature stop codons in affected skin epidermis, but high rates of wild-type transcripts in the potentially revertant area epidermis, supports this diagnosis.

rejected.label: Dystrophic Epidermolysis Bullosa
rejected.why: While the patient has a large unhealed ulcer and genetic alterations in COL7A1 consistent with this condition, the presence of a patch of healthy skin with high rates of wild-type transcripts suggests revertant mosaicism.

rejected.label: Junctional Epidermolysis Bullosa
rejected.why: This condition is not supported by the genetic findings, which implicate COL7A1, a gene associated with dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa.

rejected.label: Epidermolysis Bullosa Simplex
rejected.why: The clinical and genetic features do not align with this condition, which typically involves mutations in genes such as KRT5 or KRT14, and is characterized by a different pattern of blistering.

rejected.label: Kindler Syndrome
rejected.why: While Kindler syndrome involves skin blistering and is a rare genetic condition, the specific genetic findings and clinical features in this case do not align with Kindler syndrome, which is associated with mutations in the KIND1 gene.
